title: 2  Machine Learning
text:
2.1 Supervised Learning
Every day you rely on machine learning without noticing it: the filter that quietly moves junk mail out of your inbox, the photo app that groups pictures by who appears in them, the streaming service that lines up the next thing you are likely to watch, and the engine that taught itself to play chess better than any human. Behind each of these is the same core idea — a system that improves at a task by learning from data rather than by following hand-written rules.
Machine learning is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence focused on developing algorithms that enable computers to learn from data and to make predictions or decisions based on data.
Machine learning is concerned with the mechanisms and algorithms through which machines can improve their performance on a given task from experience, represented by the data associated with that task.
In recent years, this area has seen an explosive growth and is often colloquially conflated with AI in popular discussion.
The machine learning field can be coarsely divided into three areas:
There are a few other kinds of machine learning that are connected to one of these three main areas — self-supervised learning, for example — but those three areas cover most of the current applications of machine learning.
A supervised learning model defines a mapping from one or more inputs to one or more output predictions, based on provided examples of input and output pairs. These input/output pairs take the role of a teacher or a supervisor for the learning process, and this gives rise to the term supervised learning.
Mathematically, we can represent a supervised learning model as a function \(f(\mathbf{x})\) that takes an input \(\mathbf{x}\) and returns an output \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\):
\[
\mathbf{\hat{y}} = f(\mathbf{x})
\]
Here, boldface indicates a vector, so \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\) may each contain several values, and the hat denotes a prediction: \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\) is the model’s estimate of the true output \(\mathbf{y}\), not the true output itself. The process of computing \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\) from the input \(\mathbf{x}\) is called inference.
The function \(f\) depends on internal parameters, usually denoted \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Training (or learning) is the process of adjusting these parameters so that the predictions \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\) match the true outputs \(\mathbf{y}\) as closely as possible across the provided examples. How close they are is measured by a loss function, and training amounts to searching for the parameters that make this loss as small as possible. Once the parameters are fixed, the model can be used for inference on new, unseen inputs.
Supervised learning deals with two kinds of problems: regression problems and classification problems.

title: 2  Machine Learning
text:
2.1.1 Regression
Regression problems in supervised learning involve predicting the value of an outcome variable based on one or more predictor variables that are represented by the input data to the model. In machine learning, the emphasis is on prediction: the model learns from past examples so it can estimate the outcome for new inputs it has not seen before. This differs in emphasis from classical statistics, where regression is often used to explain the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables.
An example of a regression application is to predict the price of a house based on input characteristics such as the square footage, the number of bedrooms, the number of bathrooms, the age of the house, location, and other relevant attributes. In this case a model can learn from historical data of house sales and predict the prices of new listings.

Another example is predicting the future demand for products or services based on past sales data, seasonal trends, economic indicators, and other relevant factors in order to improve inventory management, supply chain optimization, and financial planning.
In both examples, we are trying to predict a numerical value from the different predictors.


2.1.2 Classification
In a classification application, the model returns a category assignment (a label) to the input data.
A classic example of a classification problem is to classify emails as spam or not spam based on input features such as the frequency of certain words, the email sender, the time of day the email was sent, and other relevant features. In this case, since the model attempts to assign the input to one of two categories, this is a binary classification problem.
Another example is a model that has a handwritten digit image file as an input and predicts which number is written. This is a multiclass classification problem, since there are more than two possible numbers, which are the categories of the problem in this case.

title: 2  Machine Learning
text:
2.2 Unsupervised Learning
Constructing a model from input data without corresponding output labels is termed unsupervised learning; the absence of output labels means that there can be no “supervision”.
Rather than learning a mapping from input to output, the goal of unsupervised learning is to describe or understand the structure of the data.
Unsupervised learning problems can be divided into three areas:

Clustering;
Dimensionality reduction;
Generative modeling.


2.2.1 Clustering
Intuitively, clustering is like sorting a pile of unlabeled photographs into groups by resemblance, without being told in advance what those groups should be. Clustering is a fundamental task in unsupervised learning where the goal is to group similar data together based on certain features or characteristics.
For example, in marketing, clustering can be used to group customers based on their purchasing behavior, demographic attributes, or browsing patterns, so that businesses can tailor marketing strategies and product offerings to specific segments, thereby improving customer satisfaction and retention.


2.2.2 Dimensionality Reduction
Dimensionality reduction is another fundamental problem in unsupervised learning that involves reducing the number of random variables under consideration by obtaining a smaller set of representative variables.
This process is essential for simplifying the analysis, visualization and interpretation of high-dimensional data while preserving its essential structure and characteristics. It also helps in the processing of the data since we are now dealing with a smaller number of features.


2.2.3 Generative Modeling
Generative modeling is another fundamental problem in unsupervised learning that involves learning the underlying probability distribution of the data in order to produce new samples that resemble the original data. This is closely related to density estimation, where the goal is to estimate how likely different data points are under the distribution that generated them.
For example, a generative model can learn from a large collection of images and then synthesize new, realistic images that never appeared in the training set. The same principle allows models to generate coherent text, compose music, or produce synthetic data to augment a dataset when real examples are scarce or expensive to obtain. This area has become one of the most consequential in machine learning in recent years, as it underlies much of the current progress that is now widely associated with the term AI.1

title: 2  Machine Learning
text:
2.3 Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning can be pictured as training a dog with treats: the animal is never told the correct action outright, but gradually learns which behaviors earn rewards by trying things and seeing what follows — and sometimes the treat arrives well after the trick that earned it. Reinforcement Learning is a type of machine learning paradigm concerned with how agents ought to take actions in an environment in order to maximize some notion of cumulative reward. Unlike supervised learning, where the model is trained on labeled data, or unsupervised learning, where the model must find structure in unlabeled data, reinforcement learning is about learning through trial and error interactions with an environment.
In Reinforcement Learning, an agent interacts with an environment by taking actions, receiving feedback in the form of rewards, and updating its knowledge or policy to make better decisions over time.
The goal of reinforcement learning is to find an optimal policy that maximizes the cumulative reward over time, that is, the agent learns to choose actions that lead to higher rewards on average. This is typically done by iteratively updating the agent’s policy based on the rewards received from the environment.
One complication is that the reward may occur some time after the action is taken, so associating a reward with an action is not straightforward — much like the dog, the agent cannot easily tell which of its earlier actions earned the reward. This is known as the temporal credit assignment problem.
As the agent learns, it must trade off exploration and exploitation of what it already knows; perhaps the agent has already learned how to receive modest rewards; should it follow this strategy (exploit what it knows), or should it try different actions to see if it can improve (explore other opportunities)?

title: 3  Supervised Learning
text:
3.1 Model Evaluation
Recall the house-price predictor. How does a model actually learn to turn square footage and number of bedrooms into a price? As we saw, supervised learning models define a mapping from input data to output predictions based on provided examples of input and output pairs. As said before, supervised learning models define a mapping from input data to output predictions based on provided examples of input and output pairs.
Mathematically, we can represent a supervised learning model as a function \(f(\mathbf{x})\) that takes inputs \(\mathbf{x}\), described in the form of a vector, and returns an output vector \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}\):
\[
\mathbf{\hat{y}} = f(\mathbf{x})
\]
Thus, the model is just a mathematical equation with a fixed form. It represents a family of different relations between the inputs and outputs. The model also contains parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), such that the choice of parameters determines the particular relation between inputs and outputs, so we can write
\[
\mathbf{\hat{y}} = f(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta})
\]
When we talk about learning or training a model, we mean that we attempt to find the set of parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) that make good output predictions from the input, that is, we want to find the equation that describes the training data most accurately. For example, for a linear model with two independent variables, we have
\[
\hat{y} = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b,
\]
where \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are the independent variables and \(\mathbf{x} = \left[ x_1, x_2 \right]^T\) is the vector of independent variables, or input vector, and \(w_1\), \(w_2\), and \(b\) are the model parameters, such that \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = \left[ w_1, w_2, b \right]^T\) is the vector of parameters.
We learn these parameters using a training dataset of pairs of input and output examples \(\left\{ \mathbf{x}_n, \mathbf{y}_n \right\}_{n=1}^{N}\). Our objective is to select the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) that map each training input to its associated output as closely as possible.
We quantify the degree of mismatch in this mapping with a loss function \(J\), also known as cost function or objective function. This is a scalar value that summarizes how poorly the model predicts the training outputs from their corresponding input for the model parameters.
For instance, in a regression problem a very common choice is the mean squared error, which averages the squared gap between each prediction and its true output:
\[
J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \left( y_n - f(\mathbf{x}_n, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \right)^2.
\]
The squaring makes every error positive and penalizes large mistakes more heavily than small ones. Minimizing \(J\) therefore pushes the predictions \(f(\mathbf{x}_n, \boldsymbol{\theta})\) toward the true values \(y_n\).
We can then consider the loss as a function of the parameters \(J(\boldsymbol{\theta})\), such that, when we train the model, we are seeking the parameters that minimize this loss function:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \operatorname*{argmin}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\]
If the loss is small after this minimization, we have found model parameters that accurately predict the training outputs \(\mathbf{y}_n\) from the training inputs \(\mathbf{x}_n\).
After training a model, we assess it on data it did not observe during training. We use a validation set to compare candidate models and settings and to check for problems such as overfitting, and finally a separate test set to obtain an unbiased estimate of how well the chosen model generalizes. If this estimate is adequate, we are ready to deploy the model.
In supervised learning, in both regression and classification problems, each model represents a family of equations mapping inputs to outputs. The particular equation is chosen using the training dataset, which are examples of input/output pairs used to choose the best model parameters.
The process of training a supervised learning model involves using a learning algorithm to adjust the model’s parameters so that its predictions closely match the true outcomes in the training data.
During development, we evaluate candidate models on a separate validation dataset that the model did not see during training. This lets us compare models, tune their settings, and detect underfitting or overfitting. Because these choices are guided by the validation set, its score is no longer an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. For that final estimate we hold out a third test dataset, which we touch only once, after all choices have been fixed.
With this in mind, we split our data into three parts in all applications throughout this course: the training dataset for adjusting the model parameters, the validation dataset for comparing models and choosing their settings, and the test dataset for the final, unbiased evaluation of the chosen model’s performance.

title: 3  Supervised Learning
text:
3.2 Underfitting and Overfitting
Having trained the model, we want to know whether it has captured the real structure of the data or merely memorized it. We diagnose this by comparing its loss on the training set with its loss on the validation set. The degree to which the prediction accuracy generalizes to the validation data depends in part on how representative and complete the training data is. However, it also depends on how expressive the model is.
A simple model like a line might not be able to capture the true relationship between input and output. This is known as underfitting. It is straightforward to identify an underfit model: it will have a poor performance both on the training dataset and on the validation dataset.
Conversely, a very expressive model may describe statistical peculiarities of the training data that are atypical and lead to unusual predictions. This is known as overfitting. In this case, the model overlearns a dataset, to the extent of learning all the noise and errors in a dataset. Thus, the model fails to perform well for unobserved data.
We can detect if a model is overfitting the training data by comparing its performance on both training dataset and validation dataset. If the model has a good performance on the training dataset, but a poor performance on the validation dataset, then it is probably overfitting to the training data.



Underfitting, appropriate fit, and overfitting


Left: the model is too simple to capture the structure of the data (underfitting). Center: an appropriate fit. Right: the model has fit the noise in the data (overfitting).
In the figure on the left, the simplicity of the model did not allow it to capture the data structure, indicating a case of underfitting. In the center figure, we have an ideal fit. In the figure on the right, we observe that the model started to fit to the noise present in the data, representing a case of overfitting.




Training and validation loss versus model complexity


Figure: As model complexity increases, training loss keeps falling while validation loss falls and then rises. The gap between the two curves widens in the overfitting regime.
This figure summarizes the tension between underfitting and overfitting in a single picture. The horizontal axis represents model complexity — roughly, how expressive the model is, or how many parameters it can use to bend itself to the data. The vertical axis shows the loss, so lower is better.
As complexity increases, the training loss (solid curve) falls steadily: a more expressive model can always fit the training examples at least as well as a simpler one, and usually better. If we judged our model by training loss alone, we would be tempted to keep making it more and more complex.
The validation loss (dashed curve) tells a different story. On the left, where the model is too simple, it cannot capture the underlying structure of the data, so it predicts poorly on both the training and the validation sets. This is the underfitting regime, and both curves are high. As complexity grows, the model starts to capture the true pattern and the validation loss falls, tracking the training loss closely.
At some point the validation loss reaches a minimum. This is the good fit — the sweet spot where the model is expressive enough to capture the real structure of the data but not so expressive that it starts memorizing its peculiarities.
Beyond that point the two curves diverge. The training loss keeps dropping, but the validation loss begins to rise: the extra capacity is now being spent fitting the noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set, which do not carry over to unseen data. This is the overfitting regime. The growing vertical gap between the two curves is a direct measure of how much the model has overfit — a large gap means the model performs far better on data it has seen than on data it has not.
The practical lesson is that we cannot choose model complexity by minimizing the training loss; if we could, we would always pick the most complex model available. Instead, we watch the validation loss and aim for the bottom of its U-shaped curve, where the model generalizes best to new data.
